title: Freedom to write for the band; Mood Indigo 5,000 times
summary: Duke didn't push composing but would play a member's arrangement if worthy; Procope says every Mood Indigo was a new experience.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Now, Rex Stewart told me once that Duke always encouraged his men to compose. Did he actually encourage you? Did he go out of his way to encourage you to compose, or was he just open to it?

Well, I wouldn't say that he encouraged you, but if you did have a -- you know, if you were inclined that way he wouldn't, you know, stop you. And he'd let you make your arrangement and he'd have the band play it, and if he thought it worthy to play, you know, he'd do it. If he didn't think it was worthy he wouldn't have too much to say, but he just wouldn't use it.
So I guess that is a form of encouragement, the fact that it was possible.
Oh, yes, of course. Oh, in that sense yes, yes. Yes, yes. Uh-huh.

5,000 times while I was in the band. And really, every time I played it it was a new experience, because every time you thought you'd put a little twist there, a different gliss there or something, because like everything we played in Duke's band, what you did to what you were playing added to -- you know, you just didn't play note for note what you played every night, you know.
